title: Stop first, then size
teaches: Put the stop where the idea is proven wrong, then size from that distance: shares are dollars at risk divided by risk per share, position % is risk % divided by stop %, and you move the size, never the stop.

sources.title: Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders: Investor Bulletin
Stop Orders: Factors to Consider During Volatile Markets
Master Position Sizing: Minimize Risk and Boost Investment Returns
How Stop-Loss Orders Help Limit Investment Losses and Risk
5 Elements of a Smart Trade Plan
StockCharts Insider: Why Position Sizing Sometimes Matters More Than Stock Picking (Karl Montevirgen, 2026-05-29)
sources.why_reliable: A StockCharts.com editorial article (StockCharts Insider), not ChartSchool; the author's bio on the page says he holds FINRA Series 3 and Series 34. Its MNST numbers recompute exactly ($500 / $12 = 41, $500 / $15 = 33); its NVDA share count does not (see conflicts), so only the MNST example and the general lines are cited.

The house sizing rule, section 3: Size from the stop (owner quoted)

facts.quote: The investor must then determine where to place their stop-loss order for the specific trade. For stock trades, the trade risk is the dollar difference between the entry price and the stop-loss.
facts.claim: Risk per share is the dollar distance from your entry to your stop.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Shares to buy are the dollars you will risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: Even with proper position sizing, investors can lose more than their intended risk amount if a security gaps beyond a stop-loss order.
facts.claim: A gap past your stop can cost more than the risk you planned.

facts.quote: If expecting volatility, like before earnings reports, investors might halve their position size to cut gap risk.
facts.claim: Before earnings, some traders cut the position in half to reduce gap risk.

facts.quote: For example, if an investor has a $25,000 account and sets their maximum account risk to 2%, they cannot risk more than $500 per trade (2% x $25,000).
facts.claim: Your dollar risk is the account size times the risk percent.

facts.quote: If a stock's price gaps past the stop price, the order triggers, and the stock is sold (or bought) at the next available price, regardless of a sharp price move.
facts.claim: When price gaps through a stop, the order fills at the next available price, not at the stop.

facts.quote: Start with the difference between the entry price, $67, and the exit price, $57, or $10, then divide the amount the trader is willing to lose, $750, by that difference to determine the number of shares
facts.claim: Schwab's worked example: $750 at risk divided by $10 of risk per share.

facts.quote: A more active trader may decide they only want to risk 0.5% of their portfolio, or $750 per trade
facts.claim: The risk budget is set first, as a percent of the account.

facts.quote: If they purchase 75 shares, for a total purchase price of $5,025, they'd be allocating about 3.4% of their total account value.
facts.claim: Risking 0.5% put about 3.4% of the account in the stock: risk and position size are different numbers.

facts.quote: There is no guarantee that execution of a stop order will be at or near the stop price.
facts.claim: A stop order may fill away from the stop price.

facts.quote: The biggest mistake is to decide on your position size first without calculating the space between entry and stop.
facts.claim: Choosing a size before measuring entry to stop is the biggest sizing mistake.

facts.quote: Identify the setup Determine where your trade thesis fails (this is where you place your stop-loss) Measure the distance to invalidation Size your position LAST
facts.claim: The order: find the setup, put the stop where the idea fails, measure the distance, and size last.

facts.quote: Divide your risk per trade by the risk per share, and it'll give you the number of shares to buy
facts.claim: Shares equal the risk per trade divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: In either case, place your stops where you think they'll work. Just adjust your position.
facts.claim: Put the stop where it belongs and change the size instead.

facts.quote: Some of the worst losses occur when you allow conviction to override structure.
facts.claim: Big losses come from letting conviction override the chart's structure.

facts.quote: You have $50,000 in your account and want to risk no more than 1%. That's $500.
facts.claim: In the StockCharts example, a $50,000 account risking 1% has $500 at risk.

facts.quote: Here's a real-world example using Monster Beverage Corp. (MNST). FIGURE 1. DAILY CHART OF MNST. Suppose you want to jump in now, at $86.
facts.claim: The StockCharts example buys MNST at $86.

facts.quote: If you choose the lower support level of $71
facts.claim: One stop choice in the MNST example is the lower support at $71.

facts.quote: In either case, if your trade fails, you lose around 1%, or approximately $500.
facts.claim: Sized from the stop, either stop choice loses about the same 1% if it fails.

facts.quote: But it's incredibly wide; around $38. Still, the distance doesn't matter as much as the position size.
facts.claim: A very wide honest stop works when the position is sized down to match.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop price is a trigger for a market order, not a guaranteed fill.

facts.quote: A stop order may be triggered by a short-term, intraday price move that results in an execution price for the stop order that is substantially worse than the stock's closing price for the day.
facts.claim: A brief intraday swing can trigger a stop and fill far below where the stock closes.

facts.quote: Investors should carefully consider the risk of such short-term price fluctuations in deciding whether to use a stop order and in selecting the stop price for an order.
facts.claim: Pick the stop price with normal short-term swings in mind.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: Once triggered, a stop is a market order and can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Rapid price movement during a short period of time could trigger a stop order. Due to market volatility, the stock might later rebound and resume trading at its prior price level.
facts.claim: A quick drop can trigger a stop, and then the stock can bounce right back.

facts.quote: Keep your stops too tight, you'll get stopped out a lot.
facts.claim: A stop set too tight for how much the market swings gets hit a lot.

facts.quote: For a general rule, some traders may risk up to 1%–2% of their account on a single trade and allocate up to 5%–10% of their portfolio in any single position.
facts.claim: Risk per trade and position size are two separate limits: a small percent at risk, a bigger percent in the stock.

facts.quote: because that distance determines the amount of money they allocate to a single position
facts.claim: The entry-to-stop distance, not the risk percent alone, sets how much money goes into the position.

facts.quote: Default stop: the low of the day, or the prior day's low. (Owner's answer.)
facts.claim: Our default stop is the low of the day or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: if it's a 1% stop then technically a 50% size would be 0.5% risk.
facts.claim: In the owner's words: a 50% position with a 1% stop risks 0.5% of the account.

walkthroughs.title: Stop first
steps: Find the price that proves the idea wrong. That's the honest stop, and you set it first.
Measure from your entry to that stop. That's what each share can cost you.
Only then pick the size. Picking the size first is the mistake StockCharts calls the biggest.

walkthroughs.title: The math, worked once
steps: Schwab's example: buy at $67, stop at $57. That's $10 of risk per share.
The trader will risk 0.5% of the account, which is $750.
$750 divided by $10 is 75 shares. That's about 3.4% of the account.
So risking 0.5% put about 3.4% in the stock. Risk and position size are different numbers.

walkthroughs.title: The same math in percents
steps: Position % is your risk % divided by your stop distance %.
Here's how I put it: a 1% stop on a 50% size is 0.5% risk.
That assumes you get out at the stop. A gap past it can cost more than you planned.

questions.q: You like a setup. Before you decide how many shares to buy, what do you need?
questions.why: Where your stop goes. The distance from entry to stop is your risk per share, and the size comes out of that. Size goes last.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

wrong.Your profit target: A target helps you judge the trade, but it plays no part in the size math.
wrong.A size that feels right: That's the mistake StockCharts calls the biggest one: picking a size before measuring entry to stop.

questions.q: Once your dollar risk is set, the distance to your stop decides how many shares you buy.
questions.why: True. Shares are your dollars at risk divided by the risk per share, and the risk per share is entry minus stop.
questions.lesson_line: Same dollar risk, wider stop, fewer shares.

questions.q: Finish the rule.
questions.sentence: Your risk per share is the distance from your entry to your ___.
questions.why: Stop. Trade risk is the dollar difference between the entry price and the stop. That's your planned loss per share if you're wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Entry minus stop is what each share can cost you.

questions.q: Risking 1% of your account means the position can only be 1% of your account.
questions.why: False. Risk is what you lose if the stop is hit, not what you put in. Schwab's example risks 0.5% with about 3.4% of the account in the stock.
questions.lesson_line: Risk % and position % are two different numbers.

questions.q: Which of these gives you the number of shares to buy?
choices: Dollars at risk ÷ risk per share
Risk per share ÷ dollars at risk
questions.answer: Dollars at risk ÷ risk per share
questions.why: Dollars at risk ÷ risk per share. Investopedia's example: $500 at risk over $20 of risk per share is 25 shares.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk divided by risk per share. That's the whole formula.

wrong.Account size ÷ share price: That buys everything you can afford. It ignores the stop, so your risk is whatever happens.
wrong.Dollars at risk ÷ share price: That puts only your risk amount into the stock, as if a stop-out meant it went to zero.
wrong.Risk per share ÷ dollars at risk: That's upside down. It gives you a fraction of a share.

questions.q: You'll risk $300 on this trade. Your stop is $1.50 below your entry. How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 200 shares. $300 divided by $1.50 of risk per share.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk over risk per share. Nothing else goes in.

questions.q: Your stop belongs where the trade idea is proven wrong, even if that makes the loss per share bigger.
questions.why: True. The stop goes where your trade thesis fails. A bigger loss per share just means fewer shares, so the dollar loss still fits.
questions.lesson_line: The chart picks the stop. You pick the size.

questions.q: What is our default stop on a new long trade?
choices: The low of the day or prior day's low
Where it fits the size you want
questions.answer: The low of the day or prior day's low
questions.why: The low of the day, or the prior day's low. That's our default stop, read off the chart before you size.
questions.lesson_line: Our default stop: today's low, or yesterday's low.

wrong.A flat 10% under your entry: A flat percent ignores the chart. Our default is tied to a real low the stock just made.
wrong.Where it fits the size you want: That's back to front. The stop comes first, and the size comes from it.

questions.q: Account $40,000, risking 1%. Entry $50, stop $47.50. How many shares?
questions.why: 160 shares. Take 1% of $40,000, then divide by the distance from $50 to $47.50.
questions.lesson_line: Account times risk %, then divide by entry minus stop.

questions.q: You risk 1% of the account. Your stop is 5% below entry. What percent of the account goes into the stock?
questions.why: 20%. Position % is risk % divided by stop %, so 1% over 5%.
questions.lesson_line: Position % equals risk % divided by stop distance %.

questions.q: Your position is 25% of the account. The stop is 4% below entry. What percent of the account is at risk?
questions.why: 1%. Size times stop distance: a 4% drop on 25% of the account.
questions.lesson_line: Size times stop distance is your real risk.

questions.story: You'll risk $300. You planned 300 shares with a stop $1 under entry. The chart says the real stop is $2 under.
questions.q: What's the right size now?
questions.why: 150 shares. $300 divided by $2 a share. The stop went where the chart says, so the size came down.
questions.lesson_line: Move the size, never the stop.

wrong.300 shares, stop $1 under: That squeezes the stop to keep the size. The chart says the idea isn't wrong until $2 under.
wrong.300 shares, stop $2 under: Right stop, wrong size. That doubles the risk you planned.
wrong.600 shares: Backwards. A wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk.

questions.q: A stop set inside a stock's normal daily swings can get hit even when your idea is right.
questions.why: True. A quick drop can trigger the stop, and the stock can bounce right back. Set stops too tight and you get stopped out a lot.
questions.lesson_line: Give the stop room for normal swings, then size for that distance.

questions.story: Account $25,000. You risk 0.5% on this one. Entry $80, stop $76.
questions.q: How many shares?
questions.why: 31 shares. 0.5% of $25,000, divided by the distance from $80 to $76, rounded down so you stay inside your risk.
questions.lesson_line: Round down. Rounding up spends risk you never planned.

wrong.62 shares: That's double the risk you planned. Check the risk percent.
wrong.312 shares: That's all the account can buy. It ignores the stop completely.
wrong.1 share: That divides your risk by the share price, as if a stop-out meant the stock went to zero.

questions.q: Two trades each risk 0.5% of the account. A's stop is 2% away. B's stop is 8% away. How do the positions compare?
choices: Both positions are the same size
questions.why: A's position is 4 times B's. Same risk, and A's stop is a quarter as far away, so A can hold 4 times as much. Stopped out at their stops, both lose about 0.5%.
questions.lesson_line: Equal risk, unequal sizes. The stop distance makes the difference.

wrong.B's position is 4 times A's: Backwards. The wider stop gets the smaller position.
wrong.Both positions are the same size: Only if the stops matched. Same risk with different stops means different sizes.

questions.q: Same stock, same dollar risk. Fill in the word.
questions.sentence: For the same dollar risk, a wider stop on the same stock means a ___ position.
questions.why: Smaller. More risk per share means fewer shares for the same dollars at risk. A wide stop is fine when the size matches it.
questions.lesson_line: A wide honest stop is fine. It just means a smaller position.

questions.story: Your stop is only 1% under entry, so you buy a 50% position. On paper that's 0.5% risk. You hold it overnight.
questions.q: What's the catch, if any?
choices: A gap can open well below your stop
questions.answer: A gap can open well below your stop
questions.why: A gap can open well below your stop. A triggered stop becomes a market order, and the fill can be far from your stop price. With half the account in, that hurts.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop is no license for a giant position. A stop can't catch a gap.

wrong.None, the risk is still 0.5%: Only if you get filled at the stop. A gap past it costs more than the risk you planned.
wrong.The risk is really 1%, not 0.5%: On paper it is 0.5%: half the account times a 1% stop. The danger is a gap past the stop on that much size.

questions.q: StockCharts' MNST example: $50,000 account, 1% risk, entry $86, stop at support $71. How many shares?
questions.why: 33 shares. That's $500 at risk over the $86 to $71 distance, rounded down. If it fails, you lose about 1%.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the stop from support, then let the math set the shares.

questions.story: A friend says he risks 1% a trade. He holds 30% of his account in one stock, with the stop 8% below.
questions.q: What is he really risking?
questions.why: 2.4% of the account. Size times stop distance: an 8% drop on 30% of the account. That's more than double his 1%.
questions.lesson_line: Check risk from the size and the stop, not from the plan in your head.

wrong.1% of the account: That's what he meant to risk. His size and stop say otherwise.
wrong.8% of the account: 8% is how far the stock falls to the stop, not what the account loses.
wrong.30% of the account: That's what he has in the stock. He only loses all of it if the stock goes to zero.

questions.q: Account $60,000, risking 0.75%. You buy at $125.40 with the stop at the day's low, $121.10. How many shares?
questions.why: 104 shares. Take 0.75% of $60,000, divide by the distance from $125.40 to $121.10, and round down.
questions.lesson_line: Real prices are messy. Do the math and round down, so you stay inside your risk.

questions.q: If the honest stop is too far for the size you want, nudge the stop closer so the trade fits.
questions.why: False. Put the stop where you think it will work and adjust the size. Squeeze it closer and a normal swing can stop you out.
questions.lesson_line: The chart sets the stop. Your size does the adjusting.

questions.story: Your account is $4,000 and you risk 0.5%, which is $20. The stock is $310. The honest stop is $25 under entry.
questions.q: How many whole shares fit your plan?
questions.why: 0 shares, so you pass. One share risks $25, more than your $20. The honest stop doesn't fit, so there is no trade.
questions.lesson_line: If the honest stop doesn't fit your risk, skip the trade. Never tighten the stop.

wrong.1 share: One share risks $25, more than your $20 plan. You round down, never up.
wrong.1 share, stop $20 under: That's tightening the stop to make the trade fit. The honest stop is $25 under.
wrong.12 shares: That's what $4,000 buys at $310. What you can afford isn't the test. The stop is.

questions.story: You love this setup. Your plan risks 1%, and the honest stop is 6% under entry. You want to put in 40%.
questions.q: What's the right size?
questions.why: 16.67% of the account. 1% risk over a 6% stop. Loving the setup doesn't move the place where it's wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Conviction never sets the size. The stop does.

wrong.40%, with the stop moved to 2.5%: That's back-fitting the stop to the size you wanted. The idea isn't wrong at 2.5%. It's wrong at 6%.
wrong.40%, with the stop at 6%: Right stop, but that size risks far more than your 1% plan.
wrong.1% of the account: That's your risk, not your position. Size and risk are two different numbers.

questions.story: Earnings come out tonight. You hold a full-size position with a stop 3% below the price.
questions.q: What do you do before the close?
choices: Cut the size, a gap can skip the stop
Hold, the stop caps the loss at 3%
questions.answer: Cut the size, a gap can skip the stop
questions.why: Cut the size. If the stock gaps below your stop, the order fills at the next price, not at your stop. Investopedia notes some traders halve size before earnings.
questions.lesson_line: Into earnings, your size is the real protection, not the stop.

wrong.Hold, the stop caps the loss at 3%: It doesn't. A stop becomes a market order, and after a gap the fill can be far below it.
wrong.Tighten the stop to 1.5%: A tighter stop does nothing against a gap. The open can land below both.

conflicts: Investopedia, articles/trading/09/risk-management.asp (titled 'Risk Management Techniques for Active Traders', Justin Kuepper, updated 2025-02-03, on the 2025-12-12 archive copy; the author's draft called it 'Mastering Risk Management for Active Traders'): the body says under the one-percent rule a $10,000 account's 'position in any given instrument shouldn't be more than $100', while the same page's FAQ, Schwab and StockCharts all treat 1% as the most you LOSE, not the position size. Checker 2026-11-08: the live page refuses the plain client (403) and WebFetch, so neither line could be confirmed live; the source (s5) and its FAQ fact (f09) were dropped, and q04 / q19 now cite Schwab's 'risk up to 1%–2% ... allocate up to 5%–10%' line (f33) and StockCharts (f34) instead.

Investopedia, articles/trading/09/volatility-stops.asp (James Hyerczyk, updated 2022-07-24 on the 2024-04-23 archive copy): its three quotes (dollar-amount stops 'usually hit most often', 'the best stops are placed outside of the noise', the initial stop at the level that 'would negate the purpose of being in the trade') were on that archive copy, but the live page refused the plain client (403) and WebFetch on 2026-11-08. Checker dropped the source (s4) and facts f06-f08, and re-sourced w1, q07, q12, q13, q21 and q22 to StockCharts (f18, f20, f32), the SEC and FINRA. Restore it if the owner confirms the live text.

StockCharts Insider (s9), NVDA example: it says risking '$1,000 and no more' over a stop about $38 wide 'limits you to 13 shares'; $1,000 / $38 is 26 shares (13 shares is about $500, i.e. 1%). The file never uses the 13; it cites only the MNST numbers, which recompute exactly, and the f26 sentence about wide stops.

Investopedia, 'How Stop-Loss Orders Help Limit Investment Losses and Risk': its second example says a stop 'triggers at $90, limiting the loss' after a gap down on earnings, which contradicts its own gap paragraph, FINRA and the SEC bulletin (a gap fills at the next available price). The file cites only the gap paragraph and teaches the FINRA/SEC version (q17, q24).

Investopedia, 'How to Set Effective Stop-Loss Orders' (by 'The Investopedia Team', updated 2025-10-29 on the 2025-11-02 archive copy): says a stop 10% below cost means 'your loss will be limited to 10%'. Same conflict with FINRA and the SEC on gaps. Checker 2026-11-08: the live page refused the plain client (403) and WebFetch; its two quotes (f10 swing traders' multiple-day low stops, f11 decide the stop before trading) were seen only on the archive copy, so the source (s6) was dropped. q08 now rests on the owner's own rule (h01) with StockCharts (f18), and no longer says what 'swing traders often' do.

Order of steps: Investopedia sets the account risk first and then the stop; StockCharts places the stop first and sizes last. Both agree the size comes after the stop. The file keys only 'stop before size' (q01), never whether the risk % or the stop is chosen first.

docs/study/sizing_rule.md §2 'If the honest stop does not fit the risk budget: skip. Never tighten the stop.' is credited to Toolkit problem #10, a lead and not a house source. 'Never tighten, adjust the size' is sourced from StockCharts + Investopedia (+ the SEC on picking the stop price with short-term swings in mind). The skip case is keyed only where the arithmetic forces it (q22: the honest stop allows zero shares). Owner to confirm 'skip, never tighten' as his own words if he wants it asked as our rule.

docs/study/sizing_rule.md §1 (risk 0.25% to 2%, 2% ceiling) is not explicitly marked as the owner's answer, and it is F9.01's subject; this unit states the risk % in every question instead of keying the range.

w1.notes: f18 and f17 confirmed on the live StockCharts page (2026-05-29 article), f01 on Investopedia position sizing (updated 2026-07-01). Changed: f08 (Investopedia volatility stops, live page unreadable) replaced by f01; 'the biggest sizing mistake there is' was StockCharts' opinion stated as fact, now attributed ('the mistake StockCharts calls the biggest'); step 1 now names 'the honest stop', the term q16, q21, q22 and q23 use.

w2.notes: Schwab quotes f13-f15 confirmed on the live page. Recomputed: $67 - $57 = $10; $750 / $10 = 75 shares; 0.5% = $750 means a $150,000 account; 75 x $67 = $5,025 = 3.35% of $150,000, which Schwab rounds to 3.4%. Every number is in the cited quotes.

w3.notes: h02 is the owner's quoted line in sizing_rule.md section 3. Position % = risk % / stop % follows from f02 (shares = dollars at risk / risk per share), and the owner's case checks: 0.5% / 1% = 50%. f03 (gap beyond a stop) confirmed on the live Investopedia page; it correctly caveats the 'on paper' math.

q01.notes: f17, f18 (StockCharts) and f01 (Investopedia) confirmed live; two Tier 2 publishers agree that the stop and its distance come before the size. 'Your profit target' is really wrong for the share count (it is not in the formula), and the wrong note says so fairly. Not leading: a target is a believable pick.

q02.notes: f02 (Investopedia: $500 / $20 = 25 shares) and f19 (StockCharts: risk per trade / risk per share) confirmed live. True for a given stock, which is the plain reading.

q03.notes: f01 confirmed live: 'the trade risk is the dollar difference between the entry price and the stop-loss'. Bank distractors (target, high, close) are plausible. Changed the why's last line from 'what each share costs you if you're wrong' to 'your planned loss per share', because a gap can cost more (f03), and a 'never wrong' line should not overstate it.

q04.notes: Key False confirmed: Schwab (f33, live) separates risk 'up to 1%–2%' from a position of 'up to 5%–10%', and its worked example (f14, f15) risks 0.5% with about 3.4% in the stock; StockCharts (f34, live) says the stop distance sets the money in the position. Changed: f09 dropped (its Investopedia page refuses the plain client and WebFetch, and its own body line contradicts the FAQ line quoted; see conflicts); f33 and f34 added so two publishers support the key.

q05.notes: Formula confirmed in f02 (Investopedia) and f19 (StockCharts), both live. $500 / $20 = 25 matches the page. Each wrong choice is a real error: account / price ignores the stop; risk / price treats a stop-out as a total loss; the inverted ratio gives a fraction of a share whenever at least one share fits.

q06.notes: Recomputed $300 / $1.50 = 200; calc matches. Method from f02, with f13 as a second publisher's worked example.

q07.notes: The old text ('... not where the loss feels comfortable') gave its answer away (rule 10). It now states the real cost: 'even if that makes the loss per share bigger'. Still True. Re-sourced from f08 (unreadable live) to StockCharts f18 ('where your trade thesis fails ... this is where you place your stop-loss') and f20, with f02 for the fewer-shares half. All confirmed live.

q08.notes: House question: h01 is the line marked '(Owner's answer.)' in sizing_rule.md section 2.1, read in the repo. Dropped the 'swing traders often use a recent day's low' clause and its fact f10: that Investopedia page refuses the plain client and WebFetch, and the clause was seen only on a 2025-11-02 archive copy. The why now says the default is read off the chart before you size (f18, live). Both wrong choices are real habits (a flat percent stop; a stop fitted to the size).

q09.notes: Recomputed: 1% of $40,000 = $400; $50 - $47.50 = $2.50; $400 / $2.50 = 160. Calc matches. f05 and f02 (Investopedia) and f13 (Schwab) confirmed live.

q10.notes: Recomputed 1% / 5% = 20%; calc matches. The percent formula is f02 in percent form, and the owner's own h02 case agrees. 20% is also inside the house caps, so it does not teach an oversized position.

q11.notes: Reverse case, as the unit plan asks: 25% x 4% = 1%; calc matches. The owner's h02 is the same reverse calculation; Schwab f14 and f15 show risk and position as separate numbers.

q12.notes: Recomputed $300 / $2 = 150; 300 shares x $2 = $600, which is double the plan, as the wrong note says. Changed the '300 shares, stop $1 under' note from f06 ('a stop set by dollars ... gets hit most', live page unreadable) to a line built from the story itself plus f18: the idea isn't wrong until $2 under.

q13.notes: Key True supported by FINRA f31 and SEC f28 (Tier 1, both confirmed live). Re-sourced 'good stops sit outside the noise' (f07, live page unreadable) to StockCharts f32, 'Keep your stops too tight, you'll get stopped out a lot' (live). The lesson line now says 'room for normal swings' instead of the unsourced 'noise'.

q14.notes: Recomputed: 0.5% of $25,000 = $125; $80 - $76 = $4; $125 / $4 = 31.25, so 31 shares rounded down (32 shares would risk $128). Wrong choices are real slips: 62 = the 1% answer (62 x $4 = $248, about double); 312 = $25,000 / $80; 1 = $125 / $80. Round-down lesson is correct.

q15.notes: Rebuilt. The old version (which gets the bigger position) tested the same fact the same way as q16, and its why said a tighter stop 'buys more shares'. That is false across two stocks at different prices; only the position's dollar size is sure to be bigger. It now asks for the ratio, with a calc: 0.5% / 2% = 25% and 0.5% / 8% = 6.25%, so A's position is 4 times B's.
